title: Carboplatin AUC 2 with radiotherapy
context_label: Head and neck cancer: weekly chemoradiation
indication_text: Concurrent chemoradiation for locally advanced stage III or IV squamous cell head and neck cancer when cisplatin is contraindicated or cannot be tolerated.
purpose: Carboplatin and radiotherapy are used together as part of the treatment plan for head and neck cancer. The team explains the treatment aim, expected benefit and why this medicine and schedule suit your situation.
schedule_label: Once every 7 days for 6 planned weekly doses, during radiotherapy.
schedule_summary: Carboplatin AUC 2 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 6 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar.
administration_text: Carboplatin AUC 2 is infused through a vein over 30 minutes. The dose in milligrams is calculated by the treating team using kidney function. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and prescribed anti-sickness treatment, as well as separate radiation appointments. This weekly carboplatin regimen does not automatically require the cisplatin hydration or docetaxel steroid schedule from an earlier phase.
monitoring_summary: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, plus measured kidney filtration (preferred) or an appropriate estimate for carboplatin dosing. Review prior treatment, medicines, hearing and nerve symptoms. Arrange dental, nutrition and swallowing preparation for head and neck radiation. Audiology and formal nerve assessment are arranged when clinically indicated. Full blood count and kidney and liver tests are required before every weekly cycle. Kidney results guide the carboplatin dose. Review infection or bleeding symptoms, mouth and skin pain, weight, intake and swallowing throughout radiation.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin. AUC is a prescribing target for drug exposure, not the number of milligrams in your bag; your clinical team calculates the dose using kidney function.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection

agents.name: Radiotherapy
agents.mechanism: Damages cancer cells in the planned treatment area
agents.explanation: Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
agents.watch: Report difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.
risks: Dry mouth, taste and saliva changes
Skin reaction in the treated area
Some swallowing, saliva or tissue effects can be lasting

phases.label: Carboplatin with radiotherapy
phases.detail: Carboplatin AUC 2 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 6 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar.

phases.label: Recovery and further review
phases.detail: After chemoradiation, the team reviews recovery, response and whether any further treatment is appropriate. NCCP 00419 refers to later carboplatin/fluorouracil under 00552, but 00552 is specific to nasopharyngeal cancer. It is not automatically applicable to every head and neck cancer; any further chemotherapy requires a separately confirmed indication, prescription and start date.

medicines_title: What each part of treatment does

timeline.label: Weekly carboplatin
timeline.text: AUC 2 by IV infusion over 30 minutes, if the team confirms treatment can proceed.

timeline.label: Radiation calendar
timeline.text: Attend the radiation sessions listed by your radiation team. This band does not mean radiation is delivered on every day of the week.

timeline.label: Symptoms and support
timeline.text: Symptoms can build up during treatment and continue afterwards. Call promptly if unwell.

day_groups.title: Weekly medicine visit
day_groups.body: Blood-test results, symptoms and the radiation plan are reviewed before carboplatin. The infusion takes about 30 minutes, but the whole appointment also includes assessment, preparation and any prescribed support medicines.
day_groups.action: Tell staff about new symptoms or any radiation cancellation before the infusion.

day_groups.title: Radiation appointments and symptom care
day_groups.body: Attend radiation on its own calendar, follow the mouth, skin, nutrition and swallowing plan, and record symptoms. The weekly chemotherapy cycle does not imply seven daily radiation appointments.
day_groups.action: Call if eating, drinking, swallowing or pain control becomes difficult, or if you are unwell. Keep the next blood-test appointment.

urgent_extra: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe mouth or throat pain, inability to drink or much less urine. Report new hearing changes, numbness, worsening swallowing, choking or skin breakdown promptly. During an infusion, tell staff immediately about rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
timeline_note: This is one reference week of the concurrent phase, not a complete radiation calendar. If a radiation appointment changes, contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose; do not assume chemotherapy can proceed without the radiation course.
safety_note: Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.
treatment_scope_notice: This guide covers NCCP 00419 for head and neck cancer. It does not prescribe the radiation dose or number of radiation sessions. The 6 planned weekly carboplatin doses are a separate count. Any earlier or later chemotherapy needs its own plan.
anatomy_note: The map shows where important effects may occur and which treatment may cause them. It is not a prediction that every effect will happen. Tell the team about new, severe or worsening symptoms; effects can continue after treatment finishes.
teachback: Can I explain the planned weekly carboplatin count and the separate radiation calendar? Do I know whom to call if a radiation appointment changes before chemotherapy? Do I know when my blood tests are due and which symptoms need urgent contact? Can I explain my mouth, nutrition, swallowing and home medicine plans?
passport_visit_note: Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

monitoring_schedule.note: Routine blood safety checks are different from tests ordered for a symptom and from scans used to assess the cancer. Your team supplies exact dates and explains results.

monitoring_test_details.label: Full blood count
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Checks infection-fighting white cells, red cells and platelets; low counts may require a delay or another change.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before every weekly carboplatin cycle.

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney function and filtration assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Carboplatin dosing depends on kidney function. Measured GFR is preferred where feasible, with an appropriate estimate used when needed.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before starting and before each weekly cycle. The team determines the required recency of creatinine results for the calculation method.

monitoring_test_details.label: Liver function
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Supports safe treatment review and investigation of changes.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before every weekly cycle.

monitoring_test_details.label: Hearing and nerve review
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Identifies new problems and effects remaining from earlier platinum chemotherapy.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Review symptoms before dosing; hearing tests or further examination when indicated.

monitoring_test_details.label: Dental, nutrition and swallowing assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Helps plan safe intake, mouth care and prevention of avoidable radiation-related complications.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Prepare before head and neck radiation; reassess as symptoms or intake change.

monitoring_test_details.label: Imaging and cancer assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assesses the cancer and informs further treatment.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Examinations and scans on the individual oncology and radiation plan.

anatomy: Soreness (mucositis), dry mouth and taste change may affect intake. Dental risk may persist; keep the oral-care and dental plan.
Pain or difficulty swallowing can build up and may last. Report choking, food sticking or inability to drink; ask for swallowing support.
Redness, soreness or skin breakdown may occur in the treated area. Use the radiation team’s skin-care plan and report worsening pain.
Low white cells can cause serious infection; low platelets can cause bleeding; anaemia can cause fatigue. Fever, sudden illness or unusual bleeding needs urgent contact.
Nausea, vomiting and poor intake can cause dehydration. Take prescribed anti-sickness medicines and call if you cannot drink.
Kidney function determines the dose. Report reduced urine, vomiting or poor intake; do not calculate or change the dose yourself.
Hearing change or ringing may be new or persist from earlier treatment. Report it before the next dose.
Numbness or tingling (peripheral neuropathy) may affect walking or fine tasks. Report changes and any earlier persistent symptoms.
Rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness may signal an allergic reaction. Tell infusion staff immediately.

support.title: A new support plan for this phase
support.text: Have one written list of preventive, rescue and regular medicines. Do not automatically continue steroid premedication, growth factor, antibiotics or cisplatin fluids from an earlier regimen; each requires a current prescription.

support.title: Anti-sickness treatment
support.text: The team prescribes anti-sickness medicines according to this carboplatin schedule and local policy. NCCP 00419 classifies nausea and vomiting risk as moderate.

support.title: Mouth and dental care
support.text: Arrange dental preparation before head and neck radiation. Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or difficulty opening the mouth. Tell future dentists about radiation before invasive treatment.

support.title: Nutrition and hydration
support.text: A dietitian can adapt food, supplements or feeding support to your needs. Ask for a practical fluid plan that accounts for swallowing and heart or kidney problems. Call early for weight loss, poor intake or inability to drink.

support.title: Swallowing and communication
support.text: Follow advice from your speech and language therapist on safe swallowing, exercises and textures. Tell the team about choking, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking, hearing difficulty or communication needs.

support.title: Skin and symptom relief
support.text: Use the radiation team’s skin and pain plan. Symptoms may increase during the course or persist after it ends; ask for review when care is no longer controlling them.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and other medicines
support.text: Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific contraception period. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before starting new products.

sections.title: Before the first visit
sections.text: Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.

sections.title: Time in the unit
sections.text: Carboplatin AUC 2 is infused through a vein over 30 minutes. The dose in milligrams is calculated by the treating team using kidney function. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and prescribed anti-sickness treatment, as well as separate radiation appointments. This weekly carboplatin regimen does not automatically require the cisplatin hydration or docetaxel steroid schedule from an earlier phase.

sections.title: Keeping appointments together
sections.text: Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.

sections.title: Practical help
sections.text: Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.

sections.title: Leaving the unit
sections.text: Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis
chapters.intro: Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.

items.title: Site, type and stage
items.text: Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.

items.title: Which pathway applies?
items.text: Concurrent chemoradiation for locally advanced stage III or IV squamous cell head and neck cancer when cisplatin is contraindicated or cannot be tolerated.

items.title: Tumour tests and medicine safety tests
items.text: Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.

chapters.title: Treatment choices and your priorities
chapters.intro: Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

items.title: Benefit and alternatives
items.text: Carboplatin and radiotherapy are used together as part of the treatment plan for head and neck cancer. The team explains the treatment aim, expected benefit and why this medicine and schedule suit your situation. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

items.title: When treatment changes
items.text: The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.

items.title: Understanding the next stage
items.text: After chemoradiation, the team reviews recovery, response and whether any further treatment is appropriate. NCCP 00419 refers to later carboplatin/fluorouracil under 00552, but 00552 is specific to nasopharyngeal cancer. It is not automatically applicable to every head and neck cancer; any further chemotherapy requires a separately confirmed indication, prescription and start date.

chapters.title: Preparing for and receiving treatment
chapters.intro: Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

items.title: At the treatment visit
items.text: Carboplatin AUC 2 is infused through a vein over 30 minutes. The dose in milligrams is calculated by the treating team using kidney function. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and prescribed anti-sickness treatment, as well as separate radiation appointments. This weekly carboplatin regimen does not automatically require the cisplatin hydration or docetaxel steroid schedule from an earlier phase.

items.title: The treatment calendar
items.text: Carboplatin AUC 2 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 6 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar. This is one reference week of the concurrent phase, not a complete radiation calendar. If a radiation appointment changes, contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose; do not assume chemotherapy can proceed without the radiation course.

items.title: Recording what was given
items.text: Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.

chapters.title: Between visits: symptoms and medicines
chapters.intro: Use the written home plan and contact route.

items.title: Symptoms have no safe-day guarantee
items.text: Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

items.title: One medicine list
items.text: Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

items.title: When to seek help
items.text: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe mouth or throat pain, inability to drink or much less urine. Report new hearing changes, numbness, worsening swallowing, choking or skin breakdown promptly. During an infusion, tell staff immediately about rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

chapters.title: Mouth, teeth and jaw care
chapters.intro: Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

items.title: After head and neck radiation
items.text: Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.

chapters.title: Eating, drinking and maintaining strength
chapters.intro: The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.

items.title: Recognising an intake problem
items.text: Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

items.title: If ordinary food is not enough
items.text: The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.

items.title: Fluid needs are individual
items.text: Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.

chapters.title: Swallowing, voice and communication
chapters.intro: A speech and language therapist can help protect function.

items.title: Swallowing assessment
items.text: Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.

items.title: Exercises and rehabilitation
items.text: Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.

items.title: Communication needs
items.text: Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.

chapters.title: Daily life and emotional support
chapters.intro: Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.

items.title: Smoking and alcohol
items.text: Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

items.title: Emotional and practical concerns
items.text: Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.

chapters.title: Recovery, assessment and longer-term care
chapters.intro: The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

items.title: Recovery and continuing effects
items.text: Mouth, throat and skin symptoms can continue after the last session. The team follows blood-count recovery, nutrition, swallowing and any kidney, hearing or nerve problems. Keep dental care and the agreed radiation late-effect follow-up. Scans, examinations and any thyroid or other tests follow the individual treatment plan; there is no universal scan or tumour-marker timetable here.

items.title: Cancer assessment
items.text: Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

items.title: Information for other clinicians
items.text: Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.

chapters.title: Your records and additional help
chapters.intro: Keep essential instructions available on paper.

items.title: The passport and wallet card
items.text: The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

items.title: Your urgent contact plan
items.text: Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

items.title: If you prefer paper
items.text: Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.
evidence.population: Concurrent chemoradiation for locally advanced stage III or IV squamous cell head and neck cancer when cisplatin is contraindicated or cannot be tolerated.
evidence.comparison: Your team compares this treatment with alternatives appropriate to your cancer site, stage, health and priorities.
evidence.interpretation: A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.
limitations: Research groups can differ in cancer site, stage, previous treatment and fitness.
The expected benefit and possible lasting effects must be discussed for your own situation.

consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainties, including why carboplatin is chosen and how it is coordinated with radiation. Explain low blood counts, infection and sepsis, bleeding, anaemia, nausea, infusion allergy and possible kidney, hearing or nerve effects; fertility and pregnancy; and the appointment burden. Radiation needs a separate discussion of the treated area, mouth and skin effects, swallowing, dental and saliva changes, and possible lasting effects. Confirm any earlier or later treatment separately.

questions.q: How many weekly carboplatin doses are planned?
questions.a: This source plans 6 weekly AUC 2 doses during radiotherapy, with each dose subject to safety review. Radiation has its own number of sessions and appointment calendar.
It is a target drug exposure used by the clinical team to calculate your carboplatin dose from kidney function. It is not a fixed milligram dose and is not a calculation you need to perform.

questions.q: What if radiation is cancelled or stopped?
questions.a: Contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose. This regimen is only given with radiation, and carboplatin must be discontinued if the radiation course is cut short. The teams confirm the revised plan.

questions.q: Do I keep medicines from my previous chemotherapy?
questions.a: Only if your team includes them in the new prescription. Induction steroids, growth factors, antibiotics and cisplatin fluids do not automatically carry forward.
The treating team confirms cisplatin is unsuitable and agrees the radiation and medicine plan.

questions.q: Will more chemotherapy be given afterwards?
questions.a: After chemoradiation, the team reviews recovery, response and whether any further treatment is appropriate. NCCP 00419 refers to later carboplatin/fluorouracil under 00552, but 00552 is specific to nasopharyngeal cancer. It is not automatically applicable to every head and neck cancer; any further chemotherapy requires a separately confirmed indication, prescription and start date.

questions.q: When will my mouth and swallowing recover?
questions.a: Recovery varies and effects can continue after radiation finishes. Keep pain, dental, nutrition and swallowing support and report worsening symptoms; the last session does not mean support should stop.

source_reconciliation_notes: Primary schedule and safety source checked against current downloaded NCCP 00419 v6 PDF on 2026-11-10; original PDF hash retained in sources.
Background head and neck care text retains its earlier source-check dates; independent clinical, pharmacy and patient/PPI review remains pending.

Current v6 specifies six AUC2 weekly doses and broad head/neck SCC when cisplatin is unsuitable. Its later-chemotherapy reference points to 00552, whose indication is nasopharyngeal cancer; eligibility and timing require explicit clinician confirmation, not automatic broad application. The shared gynaecology context is outside this patient draft.
